title: Rome, unhindered (Acts 28:30–31)
hookLine: Paul under house arrest, welcoming all, preaching with confidence

cards: A prisoner walks toward the capital of the world, as Luke's readers knew it.
Back on day five hundred thirty-four, at the very start of Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
Since then the story has gone out of the upper room, through Samaria and the desert road, to Antioch, across the sea to Philippi, Athens and Corinth, and through a shipwreck.
Now it reaches Rome, and Paul walks in as a prisoner.

teach.h: FRIENDS WALK OUT TO MEET HIM.
teach.b: As Paul nears the city on the Appian Way, believers from Rome walk out to meet him, at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, Luke says, he thanked God and took courage.

Even an apostle needed friends to show up. In Rome he's allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. He calls together the leaders of the Jewish community and speaks with them all day, from morning to evening.
Some are persuaded, some are not, and they leave still discussing among themselves.

Then come the last two verses of the book, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he remained two whole years in his own hired lodging; and he received all that came in to him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition."
That's how Acts ends. Not with Paul's trial. Not with his death.
The Douay says without prohibition; the last word in the Greek, akolutos, means unhindered, without hindrance.

teach.h: A ROOM, A GUARD, AN OPEN DOOR.
teach.b: A man in chains, renting a room, opening his door to whoever comes, and the word is not chained.
Why does Luke stop there? Nobody knows for certain. Maybe he wrote before the trial ended.
Maybe he wanted the story to stay open, because it isn't finished.
Catholic tradition holds that Paul was later martyred in Rome under Nero and buried on the road to Ostia, where the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls now stands. Acts itself doesn't tell it.

how: Catholics celebrate Saints Peter and Paul together on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome visit Paul's tomb at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the road to Ostia.

games.q: you're Paul, under house arrest in Rome, with a soldier at your side. you can't go out. what do you do?
o: open your door and receive everyone who comes.
games.why: for two whole years he receives all who come, preaching with all confidence. Acts ends there, on the word unhindered.

practice: Paul couldn't go anywhere, so he let the world come to him.

Picture your own small room, your desk, your kitchen, your phone, and who might come through it: an unexpected call, a neighbor, a coworker with a question, a kid with a long story; picture receiving them the way Paul received all that came in, with the door open.
If you pray, thank God for the friends who walked out to meet you when you needed it.

wordCard.voice: Rome. Where Acts ends, with Paul in a rented room, welcoming everyone, preaching without hindrance. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: unhindered, without hindrance. the very last word of the Acts of the Apostles.

carryVoice: Your line: without hindrance. And that's the Acts of the Apostles: witnesses, Pentecost, deacons, the road to Damascus, the council, Lydia, the jail, Athens, the shipwreck, and Rome. Tomorrow, the letters.
